content.text: By the eleventh month, Silvermoon had learned to live around the silence.

The magisterial annex no longer drew a crowd before dawn. Families still delivered letters, but the clerks stored them unopened in lacquered cases against a road that might never return. Outland medicines disappeared from apothecary shelves. Quartermasters dismantled the cargo wards and reassigned their crystals to the city wall. Children who had once argued over the color of Netherstorm’s sky found newer contests.

No proclamation declared Kael’thas lost. His banners remained above the Court of the Sun. Royal seals still marked old requisitions in military offices, and officials continued to speak of interrupted contact rather than abandonment. The distinction had survived so long that it had become part of the city’s discipline.
Falanaras had stopped looking toward the annex when he crossed the Court.
He was beneath the eastern barracks when the relay bell began.

The first three strokes pulled him from sleep. The next three brought him upright before thought. Across the dark chamber, Theron reached for the sword beside his cot. Daric woke more slowly, one hand going to the shoulder Sanguinar had broken. The injury had healed months ago, though cold mornings still drew stiffness through it.
The bell continued.
“That is not the failure signal,” Theron said.
Falanaras was already fastening his sword belt. “No.”
The signal for restored contact had not been used in nearly a year.

They reached the courtyard as crimson lamps flared awake along the walls. Doors opened throughout the barracks. Blood Knights emerged half-armored, carrying gauntlets and scabbards. A runner in magisterial gray came through the gate hard enough to skid on the paving stones.
“The Portal has opened,” he said. “Lady Liadrin requires Captain Dawnspear at the annex.”
Hope moved through the courtyard before anyone could forbid it.

It showed in lifted faces and suddenly quick hands. One knight laughed once, breathless and disbelieving. Daric’s expression tightened around a thought he did not voice. Sanguinar had crossed two days before the closure. Three other Blood Knights had gone with him. Whatever they had become in the silence, an open road offered the first chance to know.
The runner had not smiled.
Falanaras followed him into the waking city.

The receiving chamber beneath the annex held no travelers. Its circular platform burned with a sick green reflection cast by the relay crystals. Rommath stood within a ring of suspended sigils, both hands raised. Astalor watched the instruments beside him. Lor’themar and Halduron occupied the edge of the platform, armored as though the bell had called them straight from another crisis. Liadrin waited near the doors.
A man’s voice came through the central crystal in bursts of static.
“—field stabilized. Repeat, the gateway is active. Legion forces hold the lower stairs and both eastern approaches. We have withdrawn to the ridge fortification. Casualties—”
The crystal shrieked. Rommath closed two fingers, cutting the noise before it broke the receiving array.
“Begin again from the activation,” Lor’themar ordered.

The garrison commander’s answer arrived thinly. “Doom Lord Kazzak came out of the Blasted Lands with an artifact our magisters could not identify. He drove its power into the standing frame. The gateway answered. Demons began crossing before the field had fully formed.”
“From Outland into Azeroth?” Halduron asked.
“Yes. The first ranks secured the stairs. More followed. We could not hold the threshold.”

Falanaras remembered green fire stretching between the carved stones and blood elf pylons biting into the ground to steady it. He remembered the old garrison’s confidence, born from years of believing the route belonged to those who had forced it open. Kazzak had turned that certainty into an invitation for the Legion.
“Has any Sunfury signal crossed?” Liadrin asked.
A pause answered first.
“None, my lady.”
“The prince’s transit cipher?” Rommath asked.
“Silent.”
The Portal had reopened. The road was there. Nothing they had waited for stood upon it.
Silvermoon knew the Portal was open before sunrise.

No official notice had been posted. The relay bell had done enough, and servants carried fragments from the annex into kitchens, guardhouses, workshops, and mana lines. By midmorning the Court of the Sun had filled with families holding letters retrieved from storage. Traders reopened old inventories. Two transport factors began arguing over cargo priority beneath windows that remained shuttered against them.
The Regent Lord’s proclamation appeared at noon.

The gateway is active. The approaches remain under hostile occupation. No civilian passage has been authorized. The crown has received no communication from His Highness or his appointed commanders. Further reports will follow when verified.
Most readers stopped after the first sentence.

Falanaras spent the day at the annex with a Blood Knight guard, holding back people who believed urgency could turn prohibition into passage. A jeweler offered three months of earnings for a place in the first caravan. A mother demanded that the magisters send her through because both her sons served in Netherstorm. One young man arrived with a pack, a ceremonial sword, and a copy of Kael’thas’s earliest proclamation to the sin’dorei folded inside his coat.
“He called for us,” the young man said. “If the road is open, we should answer.”
“The road is held by demons.”
“Then His Highness needs soldiers.”
Falanaras looked at the untouched sword and the pack tied with household cord. “He needs soldiers who can reach him. You would die on the lower stairs.”
The young man’s face hardened. He left without thanking him.

Near dusk, Theron brought Falanaras a cup of watered wine and stood beside him under the portico. Across the square, citizens read the proclamation aloud to one another and supplied kinder meanings between its lines.
“They have waited a long time to misunderstand good news,” Theron said.
“There may still be good news.”
Theron drank from his own cup. “You have begun sounding like me. I object.”

The annex doors opened behind them. Rommath emerged with Halduron and four Farstriders dressed in travel leathers darkened to swallow light. No red marked them. Their weapons had been wrapped, their hair bound close, and each carried enough warding metal to burden a pack animal.
Falanaras set down the wine. “When do we leave?”
Rommath regarded his black plate. “We do not.”
“I know the far-side fortifications.”

“And every demonic ward on that plateau will taste the Light in you before your boots touch the ground. The rangers will cross under concealment, observe, and return. If the route can bear a larger force, you may resent me afterward.”
Lethira came through the doors last, checking the fletching on a short bundle of arrows.
“I offered to make his armor less conspicuous,” she said. “Apparently burying him to the neck exceeds the mission parameters.”

She stopped before Falanaras. The mockery left her face without leaving her voice. “We will look for the prince’s standards. Sanguinar too, if he has been considerate enough to stand somewhere visible.”

Falanaras wanted to tell her what dangers waited beyond the green field. She had fought through Silvermoon’s fall, Deatholme, and every blighted mile between the runestones and Tranquillien. Warnings would only name risks she had already counted.
“Come back with what is true,” he said.
Lethira drew her hood up. “That is usually the goal.”
The scouts returned on the third night with one wounded ranger and no word from Kael’thas.

Falanaras met them in a secured chamber beneath the annex. Lethira’s cloak smelled of sulfur and old blood. A narrow burn crossed her jaw. The wounded ranger lay on a table while a healer drew green corruption from his thigh in smoking threads.
Halduron stood over a map of Hellfire Peninsula. “Report from the crossing.”

Lethira placed three black stones on the map. “Legion emplacements here, here, and along the old supply trench. Felhounds patrol the lower approach. The stabilizing engines have been altered or destroyed. I could not reach the western controls without exposing the team.”
“The Sunfury station?” Rommath asked.
“Abandoned. We found blood, burned papers, and racks stripped of weapons. No bodies. The garrison may have withdrawn before the Legion arrived.”
“Or joined them,” Astalor said.
Lethira’s eyes cut toward him. “The room contained no oath of allegiance helpfully left beneath a paperweight.”
“Therefore both possibilities remain.”
Falanaras studied the map. The road from the Portal into Hellfire Citadel had once carried Kael’thas’s detachments west. “How far did you see?”

“Far enough to find every ridge occupied and no blood elf formation holding the route. We saw smoke over the northern works. Nothing flew above them except Legion standards.” Lethira removed one glove. Her fingers trembled once before she closed them. “Hellfire is open. It is not ours.”
Lor’themar had listened without moving. “You said three nights. Your planned observation required two.”
Lethira looked toward the chamber door. “We brought someone back.”

The guards admitted a blood elf woman in scorched traveling robes. Dust had turned the fabric almost gray. An unfamiliar silver eye had been stitched over her heart, and a warded case hung from both wrists on a short chain. She carried herself like a magister who had spent too many days pretending to be a corpse.
Her gaze moved across the room, caught on the red-gold light beneath Liadrin’s eyes, and stopped.
“Regent Lord,” she said. “I carry a letter from Voren’thal the Seer of the Scryers, sworn now to the Sha’tar of Shattrath. It is for your hand.”

The old name passed through the room with more force than the title that followed it. Voren’thal had advised Kael’thas in Outland. Falanaras remembered him at the edge of the Netherstorm war room, white-haired and severe, speaking rarely because the prince had listened when he did.
“The Scryers,” Rommath said. “Who named you that?”
“Those who watched us surrender and expected treachery. We kept the name.”

She raised her chained hands. “The case will open for the Regent Lord, Grand Magister Rommath, or Lady Liadrin. The cipher inside was laid before the Portal closed. Voren’thal believed at least one of you would recognize it.”
Lor’themar approached her. “Why did Voren’thal believe his word required chains and three days through Legion territory?”
“Because what he asks you to believe will sound like betrayal.” The messenger looked at the royal banners hanging above the map. “And because much of it is.”
They moved to Lor’themar’s council chamber before the city could learn whom the scouts had brought home.

Rommath examined the case beneath seven separate wards. The first yielded to Lor’themar’s touch. The next five answered old royal ciphers and magisterial signatures. The last opened when Liadrin laid two fingers against a seal formed from pale crystal.
“Voren’thal keyed this before we left for Tempest Keep,” Rommath said. “I remember the sequence.”

Inside lay a letter, three narrow dispatch rolls, and a shard of violet crystal. Astalor took the shard to a side table without being asked. Halduron unrolled the dispatches. Lor’themar broke the letter’s seal.

Falanaras remained near the doors with Liadrin. He had not been summoned as a councilor. He was there because he had walked the roads the letter described, served beneath the prince’s eye, and entered Tempest Keep with the army now accused of turning against its own future.

Lor’themar read in silence at first. His expression altered so little that each small change carried weight: a tightening at the mouth, one stopped breath, a glance toward Liadrin that ended before she met it.
“Read it aloud,” Liadrin said.
Lor’themar looked around the chamber. “What is heard here remains here until I decide otherwise.”
No one answered. He began.

Regent Lord Theron, I write from Shattrath because the truth can no longer travel through the prince’s command. I served Kael’thas as counselor, magister, and soldier. I believed his victories purchased a road home. I now believe every victory carried us farther from it.
The messenger kept her eyes lowered. Liadrin did not.

Illidan ordered an assault upon Shattrath, fearing the naaru power gathered there. Kael’thas entrusted the attack to me. I accepted command and led our people across Outland toward a city we knew only as another objective.

Before we reached its walls, a vision took me. I saw Quel’Thalas beneath a sky unmarred by smoke. Our people stood without trembling hands or hidden shame. No child watched a crystal with an addict’s patience. No mother measured the magic remaining in a room before deciding whether her family could sleep there.

At the heart of that vision shone a naaru. Its Holy Light lay over our land, and every sin’dorei it touched remembered what it was to live without craving. I felt the torment leave my own spirit. When I woke, I could no longer call our suffering permanent, nor every cruel answer necessary.
The Light within Falanaras stirred. M’uru’s presence rose beneath his breastbone, warm and wounded. He could almost hear the force-chains answering in the vault below the city.
Liadrin’s fingers had closed around the edge of the table.
“Continue,” she said.

I returned to His Highness and entered his war chamber without ceremony. Before officers who had survived Dalaran, Northrend, and the long campaigns across Outland, I told him what I had seen. I urged him to abandon the assault, seek the naaru of Shattrath, and consider that salvation might require us to surrender power rather than acquire more.

His Highness heard me with the patience he once gave unwelcome counsel. Then he asked whether a vision would feed one starving citizen in Silvermoon that night. He asked whether the naaru had offered armies, transport, or stores. He said our people had waited upon grace before and buried a kingdom for the privilege.
I answered that a warning does not become false because it arrives without provisions. He dismissed me from command.

Falanaras heard Kael’thas’s voice inside the words. The questions were cruel because they were the ones Quel’Thalas had asked of every promise. Food. Power. Soldiers. Time. The prince had once made answers from whatever the world withheld.

Those who believed me left the Sunfury ranks with me. We approached Shattrath prepared to die before reaching its walls. Instead, we laid down our weapons before A’dal and were received. We became the Scryers: servants and uneasy guests in the city we had marched to conquer.
Our departure did not turn His Highness back. I fear it drove him toward a harsher answer.

After we left, I learned that Kael’thas had broken with Illidan’s command. Sunfury forces seized the remaining wings of Tempest Keep, expelling or killing garrisons that would not answer to the prince alone, and turned Netherstorm’s engines against former allies. Supply posts vanished into his private war. Orders began carrying seals unknown to me and instructions routed through demonic intermediaries.

I cannot tell you every vow he has made, Lor’themar. I can tell you what his soldiers now guard. Legion envoys have entered Tempest Keep. Fel armaments arrive without Illidan’s mark. The prince gathers power against enemies in Outland while no longer sending relief, explanation, or command to the kingdom whose suffering justified his rise.

He has not ceased speaking of our people. That is the danger. He names Quel’Thalas in the same breath as every weapon he desires, as though our survival can sanctify an ambition that no longer returns to us.
Lor’themar lowered the page.

No one spoke for several breaths. The city’s wards hummed beyond the chamber walls. Somewhere below, power drawn from M’uru passed through conduits that still failed to carry enough relief to the districts above.
Liadrin broke the silence. “He saw a naaru above Quel’Thalas.”
The messenger looked at her. “Yes.”
“And we brought one beneath it.” Gold flared through Liadrin’s green eyes. “In chains.”
Rommath’s expression hardened. “A vision is not an instruction manual.”
“No,” Liadrin said. “It is an accusation.”

Falanaras felt M’uru’s pain within the warmth under his ribs. Voren’thal had been shown freedom from hunger through a naaru’s willing radiance. The Blood Knights had achieved relief through restraints, measured force, and obedience. Both paths passed through the Light. Only one had asked the naaru’s consent.
Liadrin turned on the messenger. “Did A’dal send this vision?”
“Voren’thal does not claim to know. A’dal received him after it occurred.”
“Does A’dal know we hold M’uru?”
The messenger hesitated. “Yes.”
The word entered the room softly. Liadrin took it harder than a shout.
The dispatch rolls supported too much of the letter.

Halduron found Sunfury unit designations beside attacks on Illidari supply lines. Rommath authenticated two command signatures and rejected a third as deliberately obscured. The violet shard held a recorded image of Tempest Keep’s outer platform: blood elf soldiers admitting a horned emissary beneath banners Falanaras did not recognize. The recording ended before any words passed between them.
“Evidence of contact,” Astalor said. “The terms remain unproven.”
“Can we question other witnesses?” Lor’themar asked.

The Scryer messenger nodded. “If your scouts can reach the marks I carried, Shattrath will send them. Some served within Tempest Keep after the closure. Others deserted when Legion agents appeared. A few still have family here and fear being named traitors before they can speak.”
“They deserted their prince,” Halduron said. “The name is not wholly inaccurate.”
“No,” she replied. “The question is whether they also deserted Quel’Thalas.”
Lor’themar looked to Falanaras. “You heard the prince name M’uru as Silvermoon’s answer. You fought under his command. Does this account describe the man you saw?”
Every face turned toward him.

Falanaras remembered Kael’thas in the war room, bright-haired beneath circling spheres, reducing an impossible assault to assignments men could survive. He remembered the prince receiving news of Rynel’s death without pretending the name meant more to him than it did. He remembered M’uru lowered into crimson force while Kael’thas watched the salvation of his people become an accomplished objective.
“I saw a commander who believed power was justified when it served Quel’Thalas,” he said. “The letter describes the same belief after Quel’Thalas ceased to limit what he would take.”
Liadrin released the table. Faint dents remained beneath her fingertips.
“He gave us M’uru,” she said.
“He sent M’uru home,” Lor’themar said. “We decided what to build from the captive.”
“Then his fall does not carry our guilt away with him.”
“No.” Lor’themar folded Voren’thal’s letter along its existing crease. “It gives us one more burden to carry ourselves.”
Rommath moved the dispatches into separate ward circles. “We need independent confirmation before making any declaration against the crown.”

“We will obtain it,” Lor’themar said. “Halduron, prepare another concealed crossing. Rommath, trace every cipher and seal. Astalor, determine whether Sanguinar or the three who crossed with him have drawn upon M’uru since the Portal reopened.”
Astalor’s mouth flattened. “The source does not distinguish distant recipients with sufficient precision.”
“Then improve the question.”

Lor’themar turned to the messenger. “You are under protective custody. You will be treated as an envoy until your claim is disproved. If you have lied, you will learn how temporary that protection can be.”
“Voren’thal expected no warmer welcome.”
“He knew us, then.”
The council dispersed near dawn. No oath had been severed. No royal banner had come down. Yet Falanaras felt the absence before any order made it visible.
By afternoon, Silvermoon knew a messenger had come from Shattrath.

The city did not know her name, what she carried, or why the annex guard had doubled. Those omissions became proof for every preferred account. She was Kael’thas’s herald. She was an Illidari assassin. She brought a cure for the hunger. She had come to accuse Rommath of engineering the Portal’s closure. By evening, someone claimed she was a high elf wearing green lenses.
Lor’themar issued a second statement. It confirmed contact with blood elves based in Shattrath and said their reports were being examined. It named neither Voren’thal nor the prince.
The restraint lasted less than an hour.
“Scryers,” a silk merchant shouted outside the annex. “They deserted His Highness and crawled to the draenei. Now they send poison home because they fear we will learn what they did.”
A veteran in a faded Sunfury sash shoved him. “If they reached Shattrath, they know the roads. Let them speak.”
“Traitors speak readily.”

City guards separated them before the quarrel became a fight. Falanaras watched from the annex stairs with six Blood Knights behind him. Their black armor and crimson tabards quieted the nearest voices without settling anything.
The elderly man who had once asked whether his daughter was safe in Netherstorm found Falanaras near the cordon. He carried the same letter. Its edges had worn soft over the silent months.
“They say the messenger came from Outland.”
“She did.”
“Did she bring lists?”
“No casualty lists.”
The man gripped the letter harder. “Then she cannot know what happened in Netherstorm.”

Falanaras could have answered that she knew enough. He could have said Tempest Keep had become a fortress against former allies, that demons entered beneath blood elf guard, and that Kael’thas had permitted Silvermoon to wait through eleven months while his war changed allegiance around him.
The evidence had not yet become a public judgment. The man before him had a daughter somewhere inside it.
“She does not know your daughter’s fate,” he said. “Neither do I.”
“The prince will know.”

It was faith without prayer, directed toward a bright-haired prince in a world most of Silvermoon had never seen. Falanaras had carried the same faith through the Portal. He had watched Kael’thas command armies, capture a living answer to their hunger, and send that answer home. The belief had never been foolish. That made its breaking crueler.
“If he does,” Falanaras said, “he has not told us.”
The man stared at him, then turned away. This time the crowd took him before a guard could guide him.

Liadrin came down the annex stairs after sunset. She had spent the afternoon beneath the city with M’uru. The captive’s radiance showed through her eyes, and exhaustion had hollowed the skin beneath them.
“Did Astalor learn anything?” Falanaras asked.

“Nothing he can defend as knowledge.” She looked across the Court, where Kael’thas’s banners shifted above citizens arguing in their shadow. “Sanguinar may be alive. He may still draw from M’uru. He may be serving the prince beside demons while carrying the power I placed in his hands.”
“You tried to teach him that strength still answers command and purpose.”
“I taught him how to reach the Light across worlds.”
The admission carried no plea for comfort. Falanaras gave none.
“What will Lor’themar do?”
“Verify every line. Summon everyone who still has the right to object. Then decide whether loyalty to Kael’thas has become disloyalty to Quel’Thalas.”

Above them, the royal banners moved in the evening air. No one had ordered them lowered. People still gathered beneath the phoenix and spoke of reopened roads, returning armies, and the prince who would explain everything when his message finally came.
After nearly a year, Silvermoon had received its first true word from Outland.
It had come from those who abandoned Kael’thas, warning that Kael’thas had abandoned them first.
